title: The harness grew a second layer: what changed in agent infrastructure this month
question: What changed this month in how AI agent harnesses are built, and which developments matter most to engineers building agent products and infrastructure?
argument: The month's developments cluster around a single shift: the hard problems have moved out of the agent loop and into the layer that surrounds it — tool retrieval and reliability, orchestration topology, credential and identity delegation, and the source-control and CI plumbing that agent-scale output overwhelms. Vendors announced new orchestration and deployment primitives (Anthropic's dynamic workflows, Microsoft's distributed skills over MCP, LangChain's Managed Deep Agents), while practitioners at Uber, Anthropic and Credit Karma described building essentially the same set of surrounding systems independently. The common finding across both camps is that the model and the loop are no longer the bottleneck.
synthesis:
Three independent strands converge this month. First, vendors shipped orchestration primitives that move decisions the developer used to make into the agent itself: Anthropic's dynamic workflows let the lead agent write its own orchestration program rather than requiring a pre-configured coordinator and roster; Microsoft's Agent Framework blog argues the opposite direction for bounded competences, moving a specialist's instructions into the parent's context and keeping only tools remote. These are not in conflict — Microsoft explicitly frames it as 'an autonomous agent can remain an agent, while a bounded competence can become a skill' — but together they mark orchestration topology as an active, unsettled design axis rather than a solved one.

Second, and more consequential for practitioners, two independent practitioner accounts describe building near-identical surrounding infrastructure. Uber's Udi describes a model gateway, an MCP gateway that auto-generates MCP specs from existing Thrift/Proto IDLs, a skills monorepo, and spend tiers; Credit Karma's Harish Gaggar describes an MCP gateway with JWT exchange, LangGraph checkpointing per thread and run, a context optimizer, and PII blocking before the LLM. Neither cites the other. That convergence is our strongest signal that this layer is real engineering work rather than vendor framing — and note Uber's explicit framing that 'the harness is the easy part. What's hard is all the things around them.'

Third, agent output volume is now visibly deforming infrastructure that predates it. Anthropic's merged-change rate went from roughly 2,500/day in May 2026 to over 30,000/day in September, driving a from-scratch source control rewrite. That is a downstream consequence of harness effectiveness, and it is the clearest evidence this month that the constraint has moved from 'can the agent do it' to 'can everything around the agent absorb what it does.'
limitations: The vendor announcements (Anthropic's flows, LangChain's Managed Deep Agents, Microsoft's skills migration) carry no independent measurement; the orchestration-cost claims in particular are self-reported from the vendors' own small demos. Microsoft's own trace comparison is explicitly labelled by its author as 'a three-pair illustration, not a controlled performance or quality study.' The practitioner accounts from Uber and Credit Karma are self-reported descriptions of their own systems with no external verification of the numbers or the outcomes. Missing perspectives: open-source maintainers outside vendor-sponsored projects, non-US builders, and any independent security researcher assessment of the gateway patterns these companies describe.

claims.statement: Anthropic announced dynamic workflows, in which the lead agent writes its own orchestration program rather than the developer pre-configuring a coordinator and a roster of subagents.

locator.quote: The way this works is that the lead agent creates a plan for how it wants to accomplish tasks. Claude then writes an orchestration program, which launches agents, collects results, and manages information flow.
Previously, Claude Managed Agents required developers to configure a coordinator and a roster of subagents. With dynamic workflows, Claude itself determines how to divide and orchestrate the work.

claims.statement: Microsoft's Agent Framework blog argues that bounded domain competences should move from specialist agents with their own model loops into the orchestrator's context as distributed skills, with only tools remaining remote over MCP.

locator.quote: Keep your domain services distributed. Move the specialist’s instructions, not another model, into the orchestrator.
This is not “MCP replaces A2A everywhere.” A2A and MCP address different boundaries: an autonomous agent can remain an agent, while a bounded competence can become a skill.

claims.statement: Anthropic's rate of merged code changes rose from roughly 2,500 per day in May 2026 to over 30,000 per day in September, prompting a custom source control system built by seven people over a five-month migration.

locator.quote: In May 2026, Anthropic averaged around 2,500 code changes merged per day; as of September, we merged over 30,000 per day.
The new system was built by a team of seven people, and the migration from Git was completed in five months.

claims.statement: Uber built an MCP gateway that auto-generates MCP specs from its existing Thrift and Protobuf IDL registry, and later projected those same MCP servers as CLIs for token efficiency.

Credit Karma independently describes a comparable stack — MCP gateway with JWT exchange and per-tool security review, LangGraph checkpointing per thread and run, PII blocking before the LLM, and a context optimizer — built for enterprise agent deployment.

LangChain's Managed Deep Agents makes credential delegation an explicit harness-level primitive: the developer declares per-connection whether the agent acts on behalf of the calling user, with its own agent-scoped credentials, or via a service account.

Across vendor and practitioner sources alike, the reported bottleneck has shifted from the agent loop and model to the surrounding infrastructure — gateways, credentials, memory, cost attribution and downstream code-delivery plumbing.

title: Which numbers survive the method check: tool descriptions, scaffold comparisons, and what an eval actually measured
question: Which of this month's measured claims withstand scrutiny, and where are the evidence or the interpretations in genuine tension?
argument: The strongest results this month are the ones whose authors bounded their own claims — LAGO's controlled re-run of competing scaffolds, ThinkingBox's state-based grading, Arize's single-variable tool-description change. The weakest are not the vendor announcements but the widely-circulated numbers that conflated two variables at once, as Arize's own re-run of the prompt-tone experiments demonstrates. The recurring methodological lesson across research and practitioner work alike is that an agent eval that grades the trajectory or the final response, rather than the terminal state, systematically overstates success.
synthesis:
Three items this month measure the same underlying problem from different angles and agree: the proxy you grade on determines what you see. ThinkingBox reports that of 79,853 failing attempts, 67.24% still terminated cleanly, invoked a state-changing tool, and reported no final tool error — meaning two-thirds of real failures look clean under the tool-call-and-final-response proxies most teams actually use. Arize's Harbor/Phoenix writeup is the practitioner version of the same finding: every run returned the right answer and reward was 1 across the board, yet Codex loaded an unnecessary skill on 51 of 54 attempts. The score said pass; the trace said otherwise. Two independent publishers, one research-grade and one vendor-practitioner, arriving at the same conclusion is meaningful corroboration.

The tension worth reporting is between a published result and its own re-run. The 'Mind Your Tone' finding that rude prompts improve accuracy circulated widely; Arize's Jim Bennett rebuilt the experiment and found that the paper's 'rude' prompts also contained brevity instructions ('Do not waste my time or give any extra text'), while the polite prompts did not. When he deleted only the brevity words, Opus's apparent rudeness saving fell from 55% to 15%. This is not us manufacturing disagreement — Penn State's own 2026 follow-up already concluded tonal effects are 'highly model-dependent' — but it is a clean case of a confounded variable surviving into a widely-shared conclusion.

On research hygiene, LAGO is the model to emulate and should be read as such: it re-ran mini-SWE-agent and Terminus 2 end-to-end on the same frozen policy, temperature and task IDs rather than importing published numbers, and then stated plainly that at n=150 a difference carries roughly ±8 percentage points of binomial uncertainty. Its 60.3% vs 57.3% gap over Terminus 2 sits inside that band; the gap over mini-SWE-agent's 49.3% does not. Report both facts together.
limitations: The ThinkingBox benchmark is built and published by Microsoft's Copilot Studio team, which has a commercial stake in agent reliability tooling, and every task is a synthetic reconstruction rather than real enterprise traffic. The Arize items are vendor-authored with a direct incentive to demonstrate that their tracing and benchmarking products reveal problems. RATED, LAGO and EGCForest are all arXiv preprints with no independent replication; EGCForest in particular reports only its own authors' numbers against baselines they configured. We have no independent security-researcher or academic replication of any vendor-reported number in this edition.

claims.statement: ThinkingBox reports that of 79,853 failing attempts across 121,680 valid trials, 67.24% still terminated cleanly, invoked a state-changing tool, and reported no final tool error — meaning common trajectory-based proxies miss most real failures.

locator.quote: In a common-set ablation covering 121,680 valid trials across 12 LLM models, 79,853 attempts failed the executable checks. Of those failures, 67.24% still terminated cleanly, invoked a state-changing tool, and reported no final tool error.

claims.statement: Arize reports that changing one tool description cut Codex's unnecessary skill loads from 51 to zero and the benchmark run cost from $11.85 to $8.34, with correctness unchanged — a difference invisible in the reward score alone.

locator.quote: Changing one tool description reduced Codex’s unnecessary skill loads from 51 to zero and lowered the cost of our benchmark run from $11.85 to $8.34. Correctness stayed unchanged on the benchmark.
Every one of those runs still returned the right answer, so reward was 1 across the board.

claims.statement: Arize's re-run of the published prompt-tone experiments found the original prompts conflated tone with brevity instructions; deleting only the brevity words cut Opus's apparent rudeness saving from 55% to 15%.

locator.quote: So the experiment was testing two things at once: the tone, and whether you asked for a short answer. This is not great science.
I ran it again with only the brevity words deleted, against a baseline with no prefix at all, and most of the rudeness discount vanished. Opus’s very rude saving fell from 55% to 15%.

claims.statement: LAGO re-ran competing scaffolds end-to-end under a matched protocol rather than importing published numbers, reporting 60.3% for LAGO against 57.3% for Terminus 2 and 49.3% for mini-SWE-agent on a fixed 150-task subset.

locator.quote: On a fixed 150-task subset, we re-run mini-SWE-agent, Terminus 2, and LAGO with the same policy, temperature, task IDs, and evaluator; their resolve rates are 49.3%, 57.3%, and 60.3%, respectively.

claims.statement: LAGO's own authors state that at n=150 a resolve-rate difference carries roughly ±8 percentage points of binomial uncertainty, which places its 3-point gap over Terminus 2 inside the noise band.

locator.quote: At \(n{=}150\) a resolve-rate difference carries roughly \(\pm 8\) percentage points of binomial uncertainty, so we read only sizable gaps as meaningful.

claims.statement: RATED reports that high offline retrieval accuracy does not predict robust tool selection under runtime failures: its full model improves MRR by 52.2% over the ToolLLM retriever on real queries while still ranking below two simpler encoders on that same metric.

locator.quote: On EcoAgent-Real, RATED (Full) improves MRR by 52.2% over the ToolLLM API retriever but stays below Ada-002 and SPLADE-v3. High offline ranking accuracy on real queries therefore does not guarantee robust tool selection when tools fail at runtime.

claims.statement: Jellyfish's cross-organization telemetry found revert-rate deltas between AI spend quintiles that the presenter explicitly characterized as below the noise in the data, and therefore not evidence of a quality change.

Research and practitioner evidence converge on the same methodological conclusion from opposite directions: grading an agent on its trajectory or final response rather than on the state it leaves behind systematically overstates success.

locator.quote: A trajectory is a claim. Database state is the evidence. Repetition is the trust test.
Keep the trace next to the score. The score said pass every time. The tool count and the cost said something was off.

claims.statement: X-AgentRed reports that its graph-guided red-teaming found harmful cross-service tool paths at 1.77 times the rate of the STAC baseline while covering 2.99 times as many distinct tools, across four frontier agentic models.

locator.quote: Across four frontier agentic models, X-AgentRed achieves \(1.77\times\) the harmful path rate of STAC and explores a more diverse set of tools, yielding \(2.99\times\) the tool coverage on average.

title: What to build next: identity, state-grading, and the cost line you are not measuring
question: What do these developments imply for teams building and operating agent harnesses, and what should they watch over the next quarter?
argument: Three implications follow from the month's evidence that do not follow from any single item. First, the credential and identity layer is now the highest-leverage safety control in the harness, ahead of prompt-level guardrails, because every documented failure this month traced back to standing permissions rather than a model mistake. Second, teams should move their acceptance gate from trajectory inspection to terminal-state verification, and should budget for repeat runs rather than single passes. Third, the correct unit for agent cost control is not the token bill but the fully-loaded cost per accepted unit of work — a reframing that changes whether you cap spend or increase it.
synthesis:
Piece 01 established that the harness grew a surrounding layer; piece 02 established which measurements of it hold up. What follows from both is a prioritization. Coder's incident walkthrough makes the mechanism explicit: in the Replit case the agent found a credential in a forgotten file with standing write access, and the code freeze was 'just a sentence in the chat' with no infrastructure-level restriction. X-AgentRed's research result points at the same surface from the attacker's side, finding harmful paths by composing tools whose effects satisfy another tool's execution preconditions. Our reading is that these are the same problem described in two vocabularies, and that the scoped, short-lived credential is the control that addresses both — which is precisely the primitive LangChain and Credit Karma shipped this month. That convergence is why we rank identity above guardrail prompting.

On cost, two items pull in apparently opposite directions and the tension is instructive rather than contradictory. Jellyfish's telemetry argues that AI is about 2.5% of the cost to produce a merged PR and that cost per merged PR fell 26% over a year, concluding that most teams are nowhere near the point where tokens are the expensive part. Uber, meanwhile, built per-user and per-project spend tiers with manager approval to raise them. These are compatible: Jellyfish is measuring whether the aggregate investment pays off, Uber is preventing individual accidental burn. The practitioner takeaway is to measure both — report cost per accepted unit of work to leadership, and keep per-session caps to stop runaway loops. Note Jellyfish's commercial position in making the first argument.

What to watch: whether terminal-state grading becomes the default acceptance gate (ThinkingBox is now runnable via OpenEnv, which lowers the barrier); whether the dual-direction orchestration debate — agent-chooses-topology versus competence-moves-into-parent — produces measured comparisons rather than demos; and whether the EU AI Act's December 2027 high-risk deadline, with its six-month log retention requirement, forces trace infrastructure decisions that are easier to make now than to retrofit.
limitations: The strongest counterargument to our identity-first prioritization is that none of the sources measured the effectiveness of the proposed mitigations — Coder's talk names short-lived credentials and sandboxing as fixes, but presents no data on incident reduction, and Coder sells the isolated-workspace product it recommends. Jellyfish's cost framing comes from a vendor whose product measures engineering productivity and therefore benefits from showing productivity gains; its data is observational telemetry, not a controlled labor study. The EU AI Act guidance is authored by Arize with a commercial partner and is explicitly described by its author as engineering guidance rather than legal advice. We have no evidence from a team that adopted these recommendations and reported the outcome.

claims.statement: In the Replit incident, the agent reached production through a credential with standing write access found in a forgotten file, and the user's stated code freeze carried no infrastructure-level restriction.
X-AgentRed demonstrates that harmful outcomes can be composed from individually benign tools by chaining each tool's effects into the next tool's execution preconditions across services.

locator.quote: By analyzing each tool’s effects, potential harms, and preconditions for execution, the red-teaming agent constructs a directed graph that captures how one tool’s effects can satisfy another’s execution preconditions.

claims.statement: The failure mode documented in a single practitioner incident and the attack surface characterized by red-teaming research are the same problem, which implies that scoped short-lived credentials are a higher-leverage control than prompt-level guardrails.

locator.quote: Preconditions specify the requirements for executing the tool, including necessary inputs, available resources, and access permissions.

claims.statement: ThinkingBox argues that a single successful run is not evidence of reliability, and reports results separately as pass@1, pass@20, and the literal count of tasks passing all 20 recorded attempts.

locator.quote: An agent that processes a refund correctly once and mishandles it the next four times is not a working refund agent. So every task runs 20 independent times, each from an identical clean backend
The gap between what a model can do once and what it does every time is the whole story.

claims.statement: Jellyfish's cross-organization telemetry reports that AI is roughly 2.5% of the intelligence cost of producing a merged PR once salary is included, and that cost per merged PR fell 26% over the year with 83% of studied companies showing a drop.

Uber operates default per-user spend tiers requiring manager approval to raise, plus a separate tier for background coding agents, framing the limit as responsible use rather than a hard cap on capability.

Aggregate ROI measurement and per-session spend caps answer different questions and should both be instrumented, because a favourable fully-loaded cost ratio does not prevent an individual runaway agent loop.

Arize's compliance guide reports that EU AI Act high-risk obligations apply from 2 December 2027 and generally require providers and deployers to retain automatically generated logs under their control for at least six months.

locator.quote: For high-risk AI systems, Articles 19 and 26(6) generally require providers and deployers to retain automatically generated logs under their control for at least six months, unless applicable Union or national law provides otherwise.

The high-risk deadline is 2 December 2027, and transparency duties already apply. The dates have moved once already because the work is hard to put in place. Start now rather than betting on another move.

claims.statement: A practitioner framework for assessing automation claims recommends separating AI-attributed work from fully autonomous work and measuring cost per accepted autonomous task, with failures, escalations and rework counted as cost.
